newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Havel, Kuchma say NATO doors should be open.
newsitem.headline: Havel, Kuchma say NATO doors should be open.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma and Czech leader Vaclav Havel signed a statement on Wednesday saying NATO should keep its doors open to any state which wanted to join the defence alliance.
"The presidents are convinced it is in Europe's interests that NATO remains open to all interested countries which are ready for membership," the statement said.
The Czech Republic is expected to join Poland and Hungary in the first wave of new entrants to be invited to become NATO members at a summit on July 8 and 9 in Madrid.

Havel, speaking through an interpreter at a joint news conference with Kuchma, said former Soviet republics -- especially the Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia -- should not be barred from future waves.

Havel's comments on the first visit to independent Ukraine by a Czech leader were in a sharp contrast with Russia's position on the issue. Moscow insists former Soviet countries should not be allowed to join NATO.
"Personally I think this wave shouldn't be the last one. On the contrary, it should be the start of the enlargement process," Havel said.

"If republics which emerged from the former Soviet Union, for example the Baltic states, feel they must be in the Euro-Atlantic system represented by NATO, they are fully within their rights to apply for membership and be accepted."
Havel arrived in Ukraine on Monday and has also signed deals on economic cooperation and nuclear safety.
His visit was a further sign of Ukraine's desire to ally itself with European partners other than Russia.

Unlike neighbouring Russia, Ukraine does not oppose NATO enlargement and has an active role in the alliance's Partnership for Peace programme. Kiev has not applied for membership but several senior officials have suggested Ukraine might try to join after 2000.
Kuchma, who is going to Madrid to sign a special NATO-Ukraine security charter, said Russia's behaviour would be the main factor influencing NATO enlargement.

"I am sure these processes will be closely linked to the situation in Russia," Kuchma said. "Which way will Russia choose -- democratic, market reforms or the opposite -- will influence the speed of the (enlargement) process".
The key sticking point marring post-Soviet relations between Ukraine and Russia was officially cleared up in May when Kuchma and Russian President Boris Yeltsin signed a friendship treaty.
The two countries agreed a 20-year lease for Russia's share of the Black Sea Fleet ships based at Ukraine's Sevastopol port.
